newsitem.title: GERMANY: German oilseed crushers ready for gene-soy arrival.
newsitem.headline: German oilseed crushers ready for gene-soy arrival.

text.p: German oilseeds mills said on Monday they were prepared to handle possible protests over the arrival of genetically altered U.S. soybeans on November 5.

"we expect limited protests but we will have to wait what form they take...production schedules have not been altered ..there are customers waiting for the products," said Arnd von Wissel, board head of crusher Oelmuehle Hamburg (Oelag).
"Seed crushers have no plans to opt out of U.S. soybeans, if local consumers wish to buy other oils and meals that is an entirely different story," a source at a crusher in western Germany said.

Nov/Jan rapeseed oil in Rotterdam, at 91 guilders per 100 kilos fob mill, has a 4.5 guilder premium over soy oil, partly a result of buyer concern over soy which has boosted demand for rape, but mostly due to tight and expensive rapeseed supplies, traders said.

The first known US new crop soybean shipment will arrive at Oelmuehle Hamburg on Tuesday evening before midnight, depending on the tide, possibly bringing the first genetically-modified beans into Europe.
Environmentalist group Greenpeace said it was still in discussions if and how to stage protests against the shipment.
"Naturally we are discussing this shipment but we can't say at this stage what we're planning," said campaign coordinatior Joerg Naumann.
Developed by U.S. firm Monsanto, the beans are resistant to a weedkiller and have been approved for import.
Greenpeace campaigns against the products, citing unknown risks to human health and the environment, and a number of large German food groups have said they would not use them.
"But this is a short-term reaction to consumer concerns," a spokesman at the national crushers organisation VDO in Bonn said.
"It does not mean to say that processors doubt the safety of the new beans, or that they are negative towards the use of biotechnology in food production."

Genetically modified crops were on the horizon in a number of countries, including the EU, where applications for licences to produce or import modified rapeseed, potatoes, and maize were pending and set to win legislators' support, he said.
